name: Underground Railroad
info: The Underground Railroad was a network of secret routes and safe houses, organised from the 1780s and run chiefly by free and enslaved African Americans, that helped people escape slavery to free states, Canada, Mexico and the Caribbean.

facts.where: the United States, from the slave states north to free states and Canada (above all Ontario), south to Florida and Mexico, and by sea to the Caribbean; routes also led into Indian territories and western territories
facts.period: earlier escape routes from the 16th century; a network of safe houses organising from the 1780s among Northern abolitionist societies; growth to the Emancipation Proclamation of 1863; escapes to Union lines during the Civil War, 1861 to 1865
facts.figures: Harriet Tubman, a conductor who had escaped slavery; William Still, who kept records and was sometimes called the Father of the Underground Railroad; Levi Coffin, said to have aided over 2,000 fugitives; Charles Turner Torrey; Thomas Smallwood; Thomas Downing; Mary Meachum; Silvia Hector Webber; Frederick Douglass, a critic of its publicity
facts.outcome: estimates of those who escaped range from 100,000 by 1850 to 500,000 or more by the end of the Civil War; at least 30,000, and possibly more than 100,000, reached Canada; the network faded as the Emancipation Proclamation and the Thirteenth Amendment ended slavery

t: The Underground Railroad was neither literally underground nor a railroad: it had no headquarters or governing body, and consisted of meeting points, secret routes, transport and safe houses kept by sympathisers and passed on by word of mouth.

Free and enslaved African Americans were the main actors in the network, and most escapes from slavery had no help from an abolitionist; routes ran north to Canada, south to Mexico and Florida, to Native American lands and by sea to the Bahamas.

The Fugitive Slave Act of 1850 drove thousands of African Americans to Canada, and historians debate how many escaped: estimates run from 100,000 by 1850 to 500,000 or more by the end of the Civil War.
dyk: The first known use of the term in print, on 10 August 1842, was a joke by the African American abolitionist Thomas Smallwood, who was quoting a Baltimore constable's exasperation that fugitives must be travelling by "steam balloon" or "underground rail-road".

sections.background:
Enslaved people escaped from slavery as early as the 16th century, and many of the escapes were unaided. In 1526 the enslaved Africans of the Spanish colony of San Miguel de Gualdape in South Carolina revolted, and historians suggest they escaped to Shakori Indigenous communities. From 1689 enslaved Africans fled from the South Carolina Lowcountry to Spanish Florida. After King Charles II of Spain proclaimed Florida a safe haven for escaped slaves from British North America, they began escaping there by the hundreds from as far north as New York, and the Spanish established Fort Mose for free Blacks in the St. Augustine area in 1738. A network of safe houses generally known as the Underground Railroad began to organise in the 1780s among abolitionist societies in the North.

Under the original Fugitive Slave Act of 1793, officials from free states were required to assist slaveholders or their agents who recaptured fugitives, although some state legislatures prohibited this. The law made it easier for slaveholders and slave catchers to capture African Americans and return them to slavery, and in some cases allowed them to enslave free blacks. It also created an eagerness among abolitionists to help enslaved people, which resulted in the growth of anti-slavery societies and the Underground Railroad.
sections.aims:
The Underground Railroad sought to carry people escaping slavery to the abolitionist Northern United States and Eastern Canada. The escapees sought primarily to reach free states or Canada, and many of those who rode the Railroad considered Canada their final destination. Other routes led to Mexico, where slavery had been abolished, to islands in the Caribbean that were not part of the slave trade, to western territories and to Indian territories.

Its members borrowed the language of the railway. The people who risked capture were called passengers and those who aided them conductors; resting places were stations or depots held by station masters, and stockholders gave money or supplies. Using biblical references, fugitives called Canada the Promised Land or Heaven and the Ohio River, the boundary between slave and free states, the River Jordan. The Big Dipper, whose bowl points to the North Star, was the drinking gourd.

Believing that slavery was "contrary to the ethics of Jesus", many Christian congregations and clergy took part, especially the Religious Society of Friends (Quakers), Congregationalists, Wesleyan Methodists and Reformed Presbyterians, as well as the anti-slavery branches of denominations that split over the issue, such as the Methodist Episcopal Church and the Baptists. Groups of agents worked in organisations known as vigilance committees.
sections.events:
The first known use of the name in print was on 10 August 1842, when Thomas Smallwood, writing in the Albany abolitionist newspaper the Tocsin of Liberty, quoted the Baltimore constable John Zell on "steam balloon" or "underground rail-road". Abolitionists quickly adopted the joke as a name for the whole enterprise. The Railroad had no published guides, maps or pamphlets. Information passed by word of mouth and in coded messages, and people usually travelled at night, about 10 to 20 miles to each station.

The Compromise of 1850 included a more stringent Fugitive Slave Law. Suspected fugitives had no right to a jury trial and could not testify on their own behalf; between 1850 and 1860, 343 freedom seekers were taken before a commissioner and 332 were returned to slavery. A few weeks after the law passed, Black populations in Northern cities declined as people left for Canada. Between mid-February and early March 1851 one hundred free African Americans and fugitives fled Boston, and abolitionists in Detroit guided 1,200 people to Canada. By December 1850 an estimated 3,000 African Americans had taken refuge there.

During the Civil War large numbers of freedom seekers escaped to Union lines rather than to the North. In 1861 General Benjamin Butler kept three men who had fled to Fort Monroe as contraband of war. On 12 May 1862 Robert Smalls and sixteen other enslaved people sailed a Confederate ship out of Charleston Harbor to the Union blockade.
sections.people:
The network was primarily the work of free and enslaved African Americans, assisted by abolitionists and other sympathisers. Conductors included free-born blacks, white abolitionists, the formerly enslaved, whether escaped or manumitted, and Native Americans. Harriet Tubman, who had escaped slavery, was one of the most famous and successful conductors. William Still, sometimes called the Father of the Underground Railroad, helped hundreds of people escape, as many as 60 a month, sometimes hiding them in his Philadelphia home; he kept careful records and published them in 1872. Levi Coffin was known for aiding over 2,000 fugitives, and Charles Turner Torrey and his colleagues often transported 15 or 20 people at a time.

Thomas Downing, a free Black man in New York, hid freedom seekers in the basement of his oyster restaurant. Black mariners, free and enslaved, gave rides, information on routes and the names of trusted people. In 1855 Mary Meachum, a free Black woman, tried to help eight or nine people cross the Mississippi to Illinois; word reached police agents and slave catchers who waited on the far shore, and the attempt failed. On the Rio Grande, Silvia Hector Webber and her husband John Ferdinand Webber ferried people into Mexico, and most of the help in the south came from Mexican labourers. The Shawnee, Ottawa, Wyandot and Nanticoke are among the Native American nations said to have sheltered freedom seekers.
sections.outcomes:
Estimates of the numbers vary widely. One estimate suggests that by 1850 approximately 100,000 slaves had escaped to freedom via the network, and the professor of Pan-African studies J. Blaine Hudson put the total at 500,000 or more by the end of the Civil War. An estimated 30,000 to 40,000 settled in Canada, half of them between 1850 and 1860; more than 30,000 were said to have escaped there in the network's 20-year peak period, although United States census figures account for only 6,000.

Many arrivals were disappointed. Life in Canada was difficult, racial discrimination was widespread, and newcomers competed with mass European immigration for jobs. In 1785 the city of Saint John, New Brunswick, amended its charter to bar Blacks from practising a trade, selling goods, fishing in the harbour or becoming freemen, and the provisions stood until 1870. With the outbreak of the Civil War many Black refugees left Canada to enlist in the Union Army, and thousands returned to the American South after it ended.

Not every attempt succeeded. In 1842 a Mexican man and an enslaved Black woman fled Jackson County, Texas, on two horses and were caught at the Lavaca River; she was returned to slavery and her husband was immediately lynched. Free Black people were also kidnapped and sold into slavery, as Solomon Northup was, in what is sometimes called the Reverse Underground Railroad. Northerners, in Andrew Delbanco's words, "began to realize slavery wasn't just a Southern issue" after 1850, and the perception that Northern states ignored the fugitive slave laws was a major justification offered for secession.
sections.legacy:
The place of white abolitionists in the story is disputed. Cheryl Janifer Laroche argued that Blacks, enslaved and free, were the main actors in the Underground Railroad, and Diane Miller wrote that historians have overlooked African American agency by portraying it as an effort of white religious groups. Larry Gara argued that many of its stories belong to folklore, and that exaggerating figures such as Tubman, Thomas Garrett and Levi Coffin minimises the agency of enslaved Black people who liberated themselves. Frederick Douglass objected in 1845 to the "very public manner" in which some western friends conducted what they called the Underground Railroad, which he thought made it "the upperground railroad" and put slave owners on their guard.

Maroon communities, such as those in the Great Dismal Swamp, were another route; Herbert Aptheker found evidence of fifty between 1672 and 1864, and the historical archaeologist Dan Sayer argues that historians downplay them. The claim that quilt patterns signalled routes dates from the 1980s and is disputed: quilt historians and Giles Wright found no contemporary evidence, and scholars doubt that spirituals carried coded directions.

In 1998 Congress passed the National Underground Railroad Network to Freedom Act, and the National Park Service designates associated sites. The Harriet Tubman Underground Railroad National Historical Park was created in 2013 and the Harriet Tubman National Historical Park in Auburn, New York, in 2017. September is observed as International Underground Railroad Month.

summary: The Underground Railroad was a network of secret routes and safe houses, organised from the 1780s and run chiefly by free and enslaved African Americans, that helped people escape slavery to free states, Canada, Mexico and the Caribbean. Estimates of the numbers range from 100,000 by 1850 to 500,000 or more by 1865.

notes: End year: the lede says the network ran and grew until the Emancipation Proclamation of 1863; the article also covers escapes to Union lines to 1865 and the Thirteenth Amendment of 6 December 1865. I used 1863 for end and listed 1865 as an event. Start is c. 1780 from 'began to organize in the 1780s'.

Numbers: the article gives 100,000 by 1850 (one estimate), 500,000 or more (Hudson), 30,000-40,000 settled in Canada, 'more than 30,000' escaping there in the peak 20 years against 6,000 in census figures, and 'at least 30,000 ... potentially more than 100,000'. All given as the article gives them.
Abolition in Canada: the article gives 1833 (Britain banned slavery in present-day Canada), 1834 (1 August 1834 and 'finally abolished outright in 1834') and the 1830s. I left the date out.
Slavery in Upper Canada: 1793 in one place; the article's other statements about Canada and 1803 court ruling left out.

Left out: Revolutionary War and War of 1812 routes (Dunmore, Black Loyalists, Merikens), the Saltwater Railroad to the Bahamas, Texas and Rio Grande details, the Pearl incident and Creole revolt, and popular culture, for length and because they fall outside the main account; the article's claim that one-pot meals became soul food left out.
